article.title: Simpson’s Paradox: When Every Segment Improves but the Total Gets Worse
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: A company can improve conversion in every customer segment and still report a lower conversion rate overall. This surprising result is known as Simpson’s paradox. It occurs when aggregated data combines groups with different baseline rates and the mixture of those groups changes. Imagine two segments: existing customers convert at a high rate, while new customers convert at a lower rate. In the first period, most contacts go to existing customers. In the second period, conversion improves within both segments, but the campaign expands dramatically toward new customers. Because the second period contains a much larger share of the low-baseline segment, the overall conversion rate can fall even though each segment improved. Nothing is mathematically inconsistent. The aggregate rate is a weighted average, and the weights changed. The paradox matters because business populations rarely remain fixed. Marketing channels change, eligibility rules change, regions grow at different speeds, customer mix evolves, and models select different people. A simple total can therefore combine both within-group performance and composition effects. Analysts should inspect important segments before interpreting an aggregate trend. Standardization is one way to make comparisons more meaningful: calculate what each period’s overall rate would have been under a common segment mix. This holds the weights constant and isolates within-segment changes more clearly. Stratified reporting can also show the total alongside segment-specific results and population shares. However, analysts should not mechanically segment on every available variable. The grouping should be related to the question and data-generating process. Simpson’s paradox is especially important in experiments and observational comparisons. Randomization generally balances treatment groups in expectation, but post-treatment aggregation, missingness, or subgroup composition can still complicate interpretation. In observational data, confounding variables can create or reverse associations. A reversal does not automatically tell us which level is causally correct. Causal interpretation requires understanding how variables relate and which quantities answer the business question. When communicating results, avoid saying simply, “Conversion declined.” A stronger explanation is, “Conversion improved within both major customer segments, but the overall rate declined because the campaign shifted toward the lower-baseline segment.” That sentence separates performance from composition. The lesson is broader than one statistical curiosity: every aggregate metric is partly a statement about who is in the population. When the population mix changes, totals can move in a direction that individual segments do not. Analysts should state the population, denominator, observation window, and decision rule before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed metric from the mechanism that produced it and from the action that should follow. This makes the conclusion easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文強調，指標本身不足以支撐決策。解讀百分比、彙總結果、model drift、非顯著結果或分類 threshold 時，都必須同時確認母體、分母、比較基準、統計不確定性以及實際 business cost。只有把觀察結果與資料生成機制、決策條件分開，才能避免過度解讀。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：percentage、集計値、model drift、非有意な結果、classification thresholdは、数値だけでは意思決定を支えられない。母集団、分母、比較基準、統計的不確実性、business costを確認し、観察結果とdata generating mechanism、decision ruleを分けて解釈する必要がある。
